vignette: Julian was twenty-one when a distracted driver careened off the roadway and smashed into the pedestrian overpass where he stood with his younger sister, Clara. The collision was a violent blur that he could not sequence into a coherent narrative; he simply knew he couldn’t seem to put the frightening event into words, his mind refusing to bind cause and effect. Instead, the traumatic material persisted as a series of unblinking images. Every time he closed his eyes, he saw the exact angle of Clara’s shoulder against the twisted guardrail, the way the afternoon light caught the glass shards on the asphalt. Beneath the visuals, the smell of ruptured coolant and copper-scented blood would bloom in his nostrils, visceral and unbidden. The shock didn’t fade. His body kept reacting as if he were still standing under the bridge. When his wife, Elena, reached across the mattress to wake him, the sudden motion put him immediately on guard, his pulse hammering against his ribs before he could force himself to recognize her. Sleep became a battlefield. He tossed through the night, trouble falling or staying asleep bleeding into morning exhaustion, until the flashbacks hit without warning, suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again. What frightened him most was how completely he had lost his footing. He came to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, the steady rhythm of his post-graduation job hunt replaced by a constant state of scanning. He felt he couldn’t rely on himself to navigate a simple pharmacy aisle, let alone secure a career. This erosion of trust in his own capacity directly fueled his hyper-vigilance, making every stranger pacing down the block feel like a direct threat. His nervous system, wired by relentless threat, meant that every distant comment or suspicious gait felt immediately potent, sharpening his focus on perceived threats and family-related comments. When he noticed those suspicious figures near their apartment or overheard the comment on the radio, the immediate threat response would spike, his body locking against sudden movements before he could process the scene. The moment he noticed those triggers, his nervous system would ignite, and the shock of the bridge would flood back in unbidden sensory echoes. To stop the panic, he began avoiding media entirely, turning away from any film or news segment that even hinted at violence, and he stopped moving through the house freely. The constant threat he felt in sudden movements and sleepless nights convinced him that his body was an enemy, kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe. This perceived vulnerability pushed him to seek anchors. He found himself needing Elena’s presence in every room; being alone in a building triggered a suffocating pressure in his chest that spiked into acute threat, waking him with night sweats and forcing immediate flashbacks whenever he tried to rest. When the dread became too sharp, he would press a key against his forearm, hurting himself physically to release overwhelming feelings, a temporary grounding that left bruised circles on his skin. Yet the avoidance only deepened the trap. The sharp photographic recall and persistent olfactory ghosts forced him to avoid media entirely, turning away from any film or news segment that even hinted at violence. By refusing to let himself remember the bridge accident in his own mind, he forced the traumatic material to surface in worse forms. His withdrawal, in turn, fed the memory fragmentation; without resolution, the event remained a series of terrifying snapshots. The sharper the snapshots, the more his negative appraisals hardened, and the heightened appraisal made every distant siren feel like a direct echo of that bridge. His retreat from the world left him utterly unprepared for it, so that every new encounter with a suspicious gait or a passing comment about family felt immediately overwhelming, which in turn pushed him toward the hallway where he avoided being alone, waiting for her to follow. Now unemployed and spending his days in the dim living room of their Brooklyn apartment, Julian finally called the community clinic after Elena found a bloodied bandage on his wrist and refused to let him retreat to the hallway. He was terrified that if he sat with the memories, he would shatter completely, yet he desperately hoped someone might show him how to trust his own pulse again.
